title: SHE PAINTED HER EYES BEFORE THEY THREW HER TO HER DEATH. BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF JEZEBEL’S STORY WASN’T HOW SHE DIED.
paragraphs: SHE PAINTED HER EYES BEFORE THEY THREW HER TO HER DEATH. BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF JEZEBEL’S STORY WASN’T HOW SHE DIED.

She was a queen who commanded kings, silenced prophets, and terrified a nation. Yet when death finally arrived at her doorstep, she reached for her makeup. The story of Jezebel is not merely about a wicked woman’s downfall. It is a terrifying warning about the heart that refuses to repent—and a breathtaking reminder of the grace we must never take for granted.
“And when Jehu was come to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it; and she painted her face, and tired her head, and looked out at a window.” — 2 Kings 9:30, KJV
There is something deeply unsettling about a woman preparing her appearance while the footsteps of death are approaching.
Outside, a man is coming to end her reign.
Inside, a queen is standing before what may have been the final mirror of her life.
She knows the kingdom is collapsing.
Her son is dead.
The dynasty she helped build is falling apart.
The man approaching her palace has already killed the king.
And what does she do?
She paints her eyes.
She arranges her hair.
She positions herself at the window.
Not to escape.
Not to plead for mercy.
Not, as far as Scripture records, to repent.
She prepares to face the man who will order her death.
Her name is Jezebel.
And before you decide this is simply another story about a wicked queen who finally received what she deserved, there is something you need to understand.
The most dangerous thing about Jezebel was not the paint around her eyes. It was the rebellion she had allowed to rule her heart.
And that is where this ancient story begins to get painfully personal.
Because you do not have to wear a crown to become hardened.
You do not have to command a kingdom to become proud.
And you do not have to bow before a carved idol to discover that something other than God has taken His rightful place in your life.
Sometimes rebellion wears royal clothing.
Sometimes it wears Sunday clothes.
Sometimes it sits on a throne.
Sometimes it sits in a church pew.
And sometimes the person most desperately in need of repentance is the person who has become exceptionally skilled at looking as though everything is fine.
But to understand that final moment at the window, we need to understand the woman who stood behind it.
Jezebel was not an insignificant figure who happened to marry a powerful man.
According to 1 Kings 16:31, she was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and became the wife of Ahab, king of Israel.
Her arrival in Israel was connected to a devastating period of religious corruption.
Ahab served Baal and worshiped him. He erected an altar for Baal in Samaria and made an Asherah.
And Jezebel was not merely watching these things happen.
She actively promoted the worship of Baal and opposed the prophets of the LORD.
In 1 Kings 18:4, Scripture records that Jezebel was killing the prophets of the LORD, while Obadiah secretly hid a hundred prophets and supplied them with bread and water.
Think about that.
Men who spoke the truth about God were being hunted.
Faithfulness had become dangerous.
And the queen had turned her royal influence against the worship of the living God.
But her cruelty did not stop with religious persecution.
There was a man named Naboth.
He owned a vineyard beside Ahab's palace.
Ahab wanted it.
Naboth refused to surrender his ancestral inheritance, explaining that the LORD forbade him to give away the inheritance of his fathers.
Ahab returned home resentful, lay on his bed, turned away, and refused to eat.
Then Jezebel intervened.
She wrote letters in Ahab's name, sealed them with his seal, and arranged for false witnesses to accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king.
Naboth was taken outside the city.
And stoned to death.
An innocent man lost his life because someone powerful wanted what belonged to him.
Then Jezebel told Ahab to take possession of the vineyard.
Read 1 Kings 21 carefully.
This was not simply a woman with a strong personality.
This was calculated injustice.
Religious language was used to disguise murder.
Royal authority was used to steal property.
And an innocent man's blood was treated as an inconvenience.
Yet there was something Jezebel could not control.
She could manipulate witnesses, but she could not silence the God who had witnessed everything.
The LORD sent Elijah to confront Ahab.
Judgment was announced against Ahab's house, and Elijah declared that dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.
Years passed.
The prophecy did not disappear.
And this is where the story becomes especially sobering.
We often mistake delayed consequences for divine approval.
We keep doing what we know is wrong because nothing terrible has happened yet.
We tell ourselves that perhaps God is not concerned.
Perhaps He has overlooked it.
Perhaps we can continue living the same way.
But God's patience must never be mistaken for His permission.
The New Testament asks a searching question:
“Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?” — Romans 2:4, KJV
God's kindness is not an invitation to become more comfortable in sin.
It is an invitation to come home.
And sometimes the most frightening spiritual condition is not when a person feels convicted.
It is when a person has practiced ignoring conviction for so long that the warning no longer seems urgent.
Then came the day recorded in 2 Kings 9.
Jehu had been anointed to carry out judgment against the house of Ahab.
He drove toward Jezreel.
King Joram, the son of Ahab and Jezebel, went out to meet him.
When Joram asked whether Jehu came in peace, Jehu answered by referring to the idolatry and sorceries associated with Jezebel.
Joram attempted to flee.
Jehu drew his bow and struck him.
The king died.
Then the news reached Jezebel.
Her son was dead.
Jehu was approaching.
And she knew that the political world she had occupied for years was being violently overturned.
Now listen to how the original Hebrew describes what happened next.
The Hebrew text of 2 Kings 9:30 includes the words:
וַתָּשֶׂם בַּפּוּךְ עֵינֶיהָ
Vattāśem bappūkh ʿênêhā.
The expression describes her applying pūkh to her eyes—an eye cosmetic or pigment used for darkening or adorning them.
The verse continues:
וַתֵּיטֶב אֶת־רֹאשָׁהּ
Vattêṭev ʾet-rōʾšāh.
She attended to or arranged her head, commonly understood as preparing her hair or headdress.
The King James Version describes this as painting her face and tiring, or adorning, her head.
The Hebrew is more specific about her eyes.
But notice what the text does not tell us.
It does not explicitly say that Jezebel was trying to seduce Jehu.
It does not tell us she believed cosmetics could save her.
It does not reveal whether her appearance was intended as royal defiance, political theater, an attempt to maintain dignity, or something else.
Those are possible interpretations, not stated facts.
What Scripture does show is a queen deliberately preparing her appearance before confronting the man who had brought judgment upon her house.
And that image is unforgettable.
A collapsing kingdom.
A palace window.
A queen dressed for confrontation.
And a judgment she could no longer command away.
When Jehu entered the gate, Jezebel called out:
“Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?” — 2 Kings 9:31, KJV
That sentence was no ordinary greeting.
Zimri was a previous Israelite ruler who had assassinated his master and seized the throne, only to reign for seven days before his own downfall.
Jezebel's words were a pointed reference to that bloody history.
She was confronting Jehu with the example of a violent usurper whose reign ended in disaster.
Even in this final confrontation, she spoke as someone who understood the language of power.
But Jehu did not stop to negotiate.
He looked up toward the window and cried:
“Who is on my side? who?” — 2 Kings 9:32, KJV
Two or three eunuchs looked out.
Jehu commanded them to throw her down.
And they did.
The biblical account is brutal.
Her blood struck the wall and the horses.
Jehu trampled her underfoot.
Later, when he ordered that she be buried because she was a king's daughter, those sent to retrieve her found only her skull, feet, and palms.
The rest had been consumed.
The judgment foretold through Elijah had come to pass.
The queen who had once exercised terrifying influence over Israel was gone.
And the account closes with the fulfillment of the prophetic word.
No royal funeral restored her dignity.
No palace wall protected her.
No title reversed the judgment.
But please understand something essential.
The Bible is not teaching that wearing makeup is sinful, that beautiful women are dangerous, or that women who exercise influence deserve suspicion.
Jezebel was judged for her idolatry, persecution, injustice, and participation in the evil of Ahab's house.
Not for wearing eye cosmetics.
And the violence in this account is a specific episode of judgment within Israel's history—not permission for believers to threaten, humiliate, or harm people whom they consider sinful.
Christians are not called to imitate Jehu's violence.
We are called to follow Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Because when we turn Jezebel's story into a shallow warning about lipstick, clothing, or feminine appearance, we can miss the far more serious warning Scripture is placing before us.
The question is not whether your eyes are painted.
The question is whether your heart is surrendered.
And that question belongs to every one of us.
The successful businessman who has built an empire but lost his integrity.
The church leader who knows how to preach repentance but struggles to confess his own wrongdoing.
The husband who can quote Scripture publicly while speaking cruelly to his wife privately.
The wife who appears gracious to everyone else but carries resentment she refuses to confront.
The young person who has learned how to look spiritually alive online while feeling increasingly distant from God.
The believer who has not prayed honestly in months but still knows exactly what to say when someone asks, “How are you doing spiritually?”
Perhaps you have become very good at arranging the outside while something inside is falling apart.
You still smile.
You still post encouraging verses.
You still attend worship.
You still tell people that God is good.
And He is.
But somewhere beneath the appearance, there is a wound you have been hiding.
A habit you have been defending.
A compromise you have been explaining away.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from obedience.
A bitterness you have allowed to become part of your identity.
And perhaps the most exhausting part is not the sin itself.
It is the constant effort required to pretend that nothing is wrong.
Jezebel's final appearance at the window should make us ask a difficult question.
What am I still trying to make look beautiful when God is asking me to make it right?
That question is not meant to condemn the brokenhearted.
It is meant to awaken the heart that has stopped listening.
Because there is an enormous difference between someone struggling against sin and someone who has decided to make peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and refusing to rise.
Between confessing weakness and celebrating rebellion.
Between crying out, “Lord, help me,” and insisting, “Lord, leave this part of my life alone.”
And here is where the story takes a turn that every wounded soul needs to hear.
Jezebel's story shows us the terrible reality of judgment.
But it is not the only story Scripture tells.
There is another woman in the Bible whose life was marked by shame and moral failure.
A woman who had lived through broken relationships.
A woman who came to a well at noon and encountered a Jewish man who knew more about her life than she expected.
Jesus.
In John 4, He spoke with a Samaritan woman who had had five husbands and was living with a man who was not her husband.
Jesus did not pretend her circumstances were different from what they were.
He told the truth.
But He did not treat her as disposable.
He offered her living water.
And the woman who came to draw ordinary water left speaking to others about the One who knew her life.
Her encounter became a witness that drew people toward Christ.
Now be careful not to force these two women into an artificial comparison.
Jezebel and the Samaritan woman lived in very different circumstances, and Scripture does not present them as direct opposites.
But their stories help us see two truths that must remain together.
God takes sin seriously.
And Jesus offers grace to sinners.
That is not a contradiction.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Because if all we hear from Jezebel's story is that wicked people deserve judgment, we have not yet arrived at the good news.
The good news begins to shine when we realize that none of us can stand before a holy God on the strength of our own righteousness.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
Not merely notorious queens.
Not merely corrupt rulers.
Not merely the people whose sins have become public scandals.
All.
The religious.
The respectable.
The ashamed.
The successful.
The broken.
The person who appears to have everything together.
And the person reading this with tears forming because something in these words has exposed a battle no one else knows about.
But the Gospel does not leave us standing beneath the weight of our guilt.
Jesus Christ entered our world.
He lived without sin.
He welcomed the broken without approving their sin.
He confronted hypocrisy without abandoning compassion.
He bore our sins in His body on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The cross reveals the seriousness of sin and the astonishing depth of God's love.
At Calvary, Jesus did not excuse evil.
He gave Himself as the sacrifice through which sinners can be forgiven and reconciled to God.
And this is why the Gospel is so much greater than a motivational message about starting over.
It is not merely about becoming a better version of yourself.
It is about being reconciled to the God from whom sin has separated you.
It is about receiving mercy you could never purchase.
Forgiveness you could never earn.
A new life you could never manufacture through appearances.
The Greek New Testament uses a beautiful word in Ephesians 2:8:
χάριτί — chariti
It is a form of χάρις — charis, meaning grace.
The verse declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” — Ephesians 2:8, KJV
Grace.
Not royal influence.
Not public admiration.
Not religious performance.
Not the number of people who applaud you.
Not how beautifully you can conceal your failures.
Grace.
Not one.
We support Gospel ministry because Christ has shown us mercy—not because we can purchase His favor.
That distinction must never be lost.
There is another Greek word that brings this message even closer to home.
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite
It is the command to repent, found in Mark 1:15.
Jesus proclaimed:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered your wrongdoing.
It is not simply crying because your choices have become painful.
It is a turning of the heart and life toward God, involving a change of mind that bears fruit in changed conduct.
It is abandoning the lie that sin can give us what only God can provide.
It is bringing into the light what we have spent years trying to hide.
And it is trusting Jesus Christ rather than our own righteousness.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because some of us are not standing at Jezebel's window, but we are standing at the edge of decisions that could change our lives.
We know we need to forgive.
But pride keeps whispering, “Not yet.”
We know we need to confess.
But fear says, “What will people think?”
We know we need to leave the sin behind.
But desire says, “Just one more time.”
We know we need to return to prayer.
But shame says, “After everything you've done, how could God welcome you?”
Listen carefully.
Shame is not the voice you must obey.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance, and His invitation is real.
In John 6:37, He says:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
Read that again.
The One who knows your hidden failures is the One who invites you to come.
Not after you have made yourself impressive.
Not after you have convinced everyone that your life is perfect.
Come to Him.
With the truth.
With the tears.
With the consequences you cannot undo.
With the memories you wish you could erase.
With the sins you need to confess and forsake.
Come in repentance and faith.
And do not confuse coming to Jesus with escaping every earthly consequence.
Forgiveness does not erase the responsibility to make restitution where possible, seek reconciliation where appropriate, or accept accountability for harm done.
But the grace of Christ reaches deeper than your reputation.
And the power of His resurrection is greater than the life you have ruined through your own choices.
That is why 2 Corinthians 5:17 is so precious:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
Notice those words.
In Christ.
Not merely in a better environment.
Not merely in a new relationship.
Not merely in a religious community.
In Christ.
The transformation begins with belonging to Him.
And that is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because sin is imaginary.
Not because judgment is unimportant.
Not because every earthly story receives a comfortable ending.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem sinners, forgive the repentant, restore the fallen, and make all things new in those who belong to Him.
We must also remember that Scripture never records Jezebel repenting in her final moments.
We should not invent a hidden prayer or a secret conversion the biblical text does not reveal.
Her account ends in judgment.
And that makes the warning all the more serious.
The invitation to repent is precious precisely because we are not promised tomorrow.
You may have years ahead of you.
Or you may have far less time than you imagine.
None of us knows.
But you are reading these words now.
And while you have breath, do not treat the call of Christ as something that can safely be postponed forever.
There is no need to make yourself presentable before coming to the Savior.
He already knows.
He knows what happened when no one was watching.
He knows the promises you broke.
He knows the prayers you stopped praying.
He knows the people you hurt.
He knows the grief you carry.
He knows the difference between the image you present and the person you are when the room is empty.
And still the Gospel calls you to repent and believe.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to protect a reputation that is slowly suffocating your soul.
Perhaps you have been so busy defending yourself that you have forgotten how to humble yourself.
Perhaps you are exhausted from living two lives.
One for the world.
One behind closed doors.
And deep down, you are longing to stop pretending.
You do not need another mask.
You need the mercy of Jesus.
You do not need another carefully arranged appearance.
You need a heart surrendered to Christ.
You do not need to become famous for your faith.
You need to become faithful to the One who gave His life for you.
And if this story has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.
If God has already begun restoring something you thought was beyond repair, share a little of your testimony.
Someone else may need to know that they are not the only person learning how to return to Jesus.

And if your struggle is too private for a public comment, you do not need to expose intimate details to strangers. Bring it before God, and consider speaking with a trustworthy, mature Christian who can walk with you.
Faith is not a performance for an audience.
It is a life lived before the Lord.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with shocking Bible stories and then leave them spiritually hungry.
Not to build an audience around fear.
But to keep pointing people back to Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
There are people who will never walk into a church building this week but may encounter a biblical message while scrolling through Facebook.
A father silently battling guilt.
A mother wondering whether God still hears her prayers.
A young person questioning whether life has any meaning.
A believer who has grown spiritually cold.
A wounded soul who has begun to believe that their past has disqualified them from ever being loved again.
One article cannot replace the church, pastoral care, or a personal relationship with Christ.
But it can point someone toward the Savior.
And that is why sharing this message matters.
Not merely to increase its reach.
But because someone among your friends may be carrying a question they have never dared to ask.
Someone may need the reminder that judgment is real, repentance matters, and grace is still available through Jesus Christ.
We also want to invite you into something deeper than reading an occasional article.
These resources are intended to help you study Scripture, strengthen your prayer life, understand the Gospel, and keep growing when the emotional impact of a single article has faded.
Because lasting discipleship requires more than one powerful moment.
It requires truth that is revisited.
Prayer that becomes a habit.
Repentance that bears fruit.
Fellowship that provides encouragement and accountability.
And daily dependence upon Jesus.
Think of it as an opportunity for regular Christian generosity—an expression of gratitude and partnership in spreading biblical truth.
Some believers may choose to give from the portion of their budget they set aside for Christian ministry, while others may regard it as an additional offering.
And it is certainly not a payment for God's blessing.
You can glorify Him through obedience, prayer, generosity, service, faithfulness, and love.
These products are not the reason to give.
They are simply a way of expressing appreciation to those who choose to stand with the ministry.
The greater purpose is to help people encounter biblical truth and continue growing in Christ.
You are not less valuable to this community.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your faithful sharing of Scripture matters.
Your commitment to Jesus matters.
No one should ever feel pressured to give money they need for essential responsibilities or believe that God's love depends on a financial contribution.
We are saved by grace through faith.
And we serve because we have been loved.
Before you leave this article, I want to bring you back to that window in Jezreel.
The queen.
The painted eyes.
The approaching chariot.
The royal chamber that could no longer protect her.
For years, Jezebel had wielded power over other people's lives.
But there came a moment when power could no longer protect her from judgment.
And somewhere in that terrible account is a warning for every human heart.
Do not wait until everything is falling apart before you begin to take God's Word seriously.
Do not spend your whole life protecting an appearance while neglecting your soul.
Do not mistake the silence of delayed judgment for the absence of a holy God.
And do not imagine that the sins you have hidden from other people are hidden from Him.
But neither should you believe that your past is more powerful than the cross of Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is not merely a warning that sinners will face judgment.
It is the announcement that the Son of God has died and risen so that sinners who repent and believe may receive forgiveness and eternal life.
Jezebel's story ends with a fallen queen.
But your story does not have to end with an unrepentant heart.
You can turn to Christ today.
You can tell the truth today.
You can confess what you have concealed.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can begin making right what you have made wrong.
You can stop treating your spiritual life as something to decorate and begin surrendering it to the Lord who sees beneath every surface.
Not because you are strong enough to save yourself.
But because Jesus Christ is a mighty Savior.
If the Lord exposed everything I have been hiding, would I run toward Him in repentance—or would I reach for another mask?
Take that question into prayer.
Let it search you.
Let it humble you.
And let it lead you to the cross.
Because the greatest tragedy is not having a past filled with scandal.
The greatest tragedy is refusing the grace that calls you to repentance and offers you a new life in Jesus Christ.
Jezebel prepared her eyes to face the man approaching her palace. Today, let your heart be prepared to meet the Savior who calls you to come into the light.
